title: Linguistics: The Science of Your Superpower

lines.t: Right now, as you listen to me, your brain is doing something incredible.
It's turning vibrations in the air into meaning. Instantly.
You learned to do this before you could tie your shoes, and nobody gave you a rulebook.
The science that studies this superpower is called linguistics.
Linguistics is the scientific study of human language.
And here's a common myth: a linguist is not just someone who speaks twenty languages. That's a polyglot.
A linguist asks how language works, the way a biologist studies life instead of collecting pets.
Language is built in layers, like a ladder.
Sounds make words. Words make sentences. Sentences carry meaning. And meaning depends on context.
Let's climb.
Step one: phonetics, the study of speech sounds.
Try this. Put your hand on your throat and say, sssss.
Now say, zzzzz.
Feel that buzz? That's your vocal cords vibrating. It's the only difference between an S and a Z.
Step two: phonology, how a language organises its sounds.
Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth, and say these two Hindi words.
The paper flutters on the second word. That tiny puff of air changes the meaning in Hindi, but an English speaker barely notices it.
Step three: morphology, how words are built.
Take the word unbelievable. It's really three pieces: un, meaning not. Believe. And able.
Linguists call these meaningful pieces morphemes.
Some languages, like Turkish, can pack a whole English sentence into a single long word.
Step four: syntax, how words combine into sentences.
The linguist Noam Chomsky wrote this famous sentence.
Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.
It makes no sense at all, and yet your brain knows it's perfectly grammatical.
So grammar and meaning are separate systems in your mind.
Step five: semantics, the study of meaning.
I saw the man with the telescope.
Who has the telescope? You, or the man?
One sentence, two meanings. That's called ambiguity.
Step six: pragmatics, meaning in context.
When someone asks, can you pass the salt?
Nobody replies, yes I can, and just sits there.
We understand what people intend, not only what they literally say.
Languages also come in families. Look at the word for three.
English: three.
Sanskrit: tri. Latin: tres. Russian: tri.
That's no coincidence. In 1786, Sir William Jones noticed that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin must share a common ancestor.
Today we call that family Indo-European.
But more than two thousand years earlier, the Indian scholar Panini wrote about four thousand precise rules describing Sanskrit grammar.
His work is one of the greatest achievements in the history of linguistics, and computer scientists still admire its almost algorithmic design.
So how do children learn all this?
Babies are universal listeners. At six months, they can hear differences between sounds from every language on Earth.
By their first birthday, they tune in to the sounds of their own language.
And children don't just copy. A child who says, I goed, or two mouses, has never heard those words.
They've discovered a rule, and applied it a little too well.
In the 1980s, deaf children at new schools in Nicaragua went even further.
They created a brand-new sign language, with its own complete grammar.
Sign languages, like Indian Sign Language, are full languages, not just gestures.
Language is also about identity. Many of us switch languages in the middle of a sentence.

parts.t: मैं कल कॉलेज नहीं आ रहा,

lines.cap: "Main kal college nahi aa raha, I have a test."

lines.t: That's called code-switching, and it's a skill, not a mistake.
Linguists describe how people really speak. Every dialect follows its own consistent rules, so no dialect is wrong.
Can language shape how we think?
Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, in Australia, don't say left or right. They say things like, there's an ant on your north leg.
And so they always know which way is north, even indoors.
Language doesn't cage our thoughts, but it can train our attention.
Today, about seven thousand languages are spoken on Earth.
India alone is home to hundreds of them, from Hindi and Tamil to Santali and Nihali.
But around forty percent of the world's languages are endangered.
When the last speaker of a language is gone, a unique way of seeing the world disappears with them.
Linguistics is everywhere.
It powers voice assistants, translation apps and AI chatbots.
It helps speech therapists, teachers, dictionary makers, and even detectives.
And in India, projects like Bhashini are building technology for every Indian language.
Every language is a different answer to the same question: how do humans share what's in their minds?
So here's your challenge. Ask a grandparent for one word from your home language that has no English translation.
Share it, and help keep it alive.
Because every time you speak, you're using the most amazing tool humans have ever created.
